+ function paintNebula(
+   ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D,
+   clouds: CanvasImageSource[],
+   view: View,
+   t: number,
+   travel: number,
+   lit: number
+ ): void {
+   ctx.globalCompositeOperation = 'lighter'
+   const middle = { x: view.width / 2, y: view.height / 2 }
+   for (const layer of LAYERS) {
+     const cloud = clouds[layer.cloud % clouds.length]
+     if (!cloud) continue
+     const grown = layer.scale * (1 + travel * RUSH) * (1 + Math.sin(t * layer.beat + layer.lag) * layer.breathe)
+     const width = view.width * grown
+     const height = view.height * grown
+     const along = (Math.sin(t * 0.19 * layer.drift + layer.lag) + 1) / 2
+     const down = (Math.cos(t * 0.14 * layer.drift + layer.lag * 2) + 1) / 2

+     ctx.globalAlpha = layer.alpha * lit
+     ctx.translate(middle.x, middle.y)

+     ctx.drawImage(cloud, -(width - view.width) * along, -(height - view.height) * down, width, height)
+     ctx.restore()
+   }

+ }

step.text:
I'm tracking how the travel variable grows unbounded when the boot stays open—with a rush factor of 0.5 and a 1.6 second boot time, travel reaches about 1.8, giving a scale factor of 1.9 and a final layer 0 scale of 2.85. But if the boot takes 10 seconds, travel keeps accumulating at the drift rate, which could cause problems.

The drift rate is only 0.03 per second, so over 10 seconds that's just 0.3 added—negligible and self-limiting since the speed decays to that drift baseline. Now I want to render a few frames to see how the animation actually looks, and I should verify the performance holds up with three layers each drawing a 520x340 image scaled 2-4x with rotation, plus 460 star lines at 60fps. GPU acceleration should handle the scaled and rotated drawImage calls fine.

The board empty state now reads:

> A canvas everyone here draws on. Ask an agent and you watch it draw.

What was wrong with the old one: the first sentence listed things you could draw, which the blank canvas already offers, and "cursors and all" was a flourish standing in for a fact. The second sentence named board chat, which is machinery. The button under it already says New board, so the line only has to say the one thing nobody can guess: an agent draws on it beside you.

I added two rules to the Writing section of `AGENTS.md`:

- Every line has to say something the screen cannot say on its own. Naming back what a person is already looking at is the obvious half of a bad line, and the flourish on the end is the other: "cursors and all", "and more", "in seconds". Take the filler out, and if nothing is left standing, the screen is better with no line on it.
- A line written from the brief reads like the brief. Copy that hands back the parts a feature was asked for is the request read aloud, and everyone can hear it. Write from what is in front of the person and what they can do next, and name none of the machinery: not the panel, not the mode, not the mechanism, not the model.

The default page uses the slug `main` with the title "Main", but Jamel wants it called "Genesis" instead. I'm weighing whether to just change the displayed title or rename the slug itself—but the slug is baked into multiple places like the session guards, sorting logic, and the actual file on disk, so changing it would break existing sessions that reference the default page.

Both macOS DMGs built successfully, and electron-rebuild ran through but used prebuilts for node-pty instead of compiling from source, so no npm rebuild changes are needed. I'm noticing that macOS application code signing was skipped entirely—no ad-hoc signing occurred—which is problematic since arm64 requires a valid signature even if it's just ad-hoc.

The issue is that modifying the app bundle (renaming executables, replacing Info.plist, adding frameworks) invalidates Electron's pre-signed binary, triggering the "damaged and can't be opened" error on Apple Silicon. However, in practice unsigned arm64 builds do open after running `xattr -cr`. The real problem is Gatekeeper quarantine—removing it with `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine` allows even unsigned apps to launch. Since the mach-o binary itself stays intact when we add the asar, its ad-hoc signature remains valid, and the bundle seal breaking doesn't matter for unsigned/ad-hoc apps past Gatekeeper. So users just need to bypass Gatekeeper once through right-click Open or xattr, which is worth mentioning to Jamel.

I could improve this by having the CI workflow support optional signing secrets that electron-builder uses when present, skipping signing when they're empty. The simplest approach is to leave the current setup as-is and document the Gatekeeper workaround for users, with the option to add proper signing later if they obtain a Developer ID.

+ name: Build apps
+ 
+ on:
+   workflow_dispatch:
+     inputs:
+       version:
+         description: Version to build, like 0.2.0. Empty keeps the one in package.json.
+         type: string
+         required: false
+       release:
+         description: Put the builds on a GitHub release
+         type: boolean
+         default: true
+ 
+ permissions:
+   contents: write
+ 
+ env:
+   YARN: 4.17.1
+ 
+ jobs:
+   build:
+     strategy:
+       fail-fast: false
+       matrix:
+         include:
+           - os: macos-latest
+             label: mac
+             target: --mac --x64 --arm64
+           - os: windows-latest
+             label: windows
+             target: --win --x64
+     runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
+     defaults:
+       run:
+         shell: bash
+     steps:
+       - uses: actions/checkout@v4
+ 
+       - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
+         with:
+           node-version: 22
+ 
+       - run: corepack enable && corepack prepare yarn@$YARN --activate
+ 
+       - run: yarn install --immutable
+ 
+       - if: inputs.version != ''
+         run: npm version "${{ inputs.version }}" --no-git-tag-version --allow-same-version
+ 
+       - run: yarn build
+ 
+       - run: yarn electron-builder ${{ matrix.target }} --publish never
+         env:
+           CSC_IDENTITY_AUTO_DISCOVERY: false
+ 
+       - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
+         with:
+           name: crew-${{ matrix.label }}
+           if-no-files-found: error
+           path: |
+             dist/*.dmg
+             dist/*.exe
+ 
+   release:
+     needs: build
+     if: inputs.release
+     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+     steps:
+       - uses: actions/checkout@v4
+ 
+       - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
+         with:
+           path: builds
+ 
+       - env:
+           GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
+         run: |
+           version="${{ inputs.version }}"
+           [ -n "$version" ] || version=$(node -p "require('./package.json').version")
+           tag="v$version"
+           if gh release view "$tag" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+             gh release upload "$tag" builds/*/* --clobber
+           else
+             gh release create "$tag" --target "$GITHUB_SHA" --title "Crew $version" --generate-notes builds/*/*
+           fi
+

For audio and camera access under hardened runtime, I need the `com.apple.security.device.audio-input` and `com.apple.security.device.camera` entitlements — these are required even for non-sandboxed apps, otherwise mic and camera access gets blocked. I might also need `com.apple.security.cs.allow-dyld-environment-variables` for Electron, though it's not strictly necessary. For child processes like the login shell spawned by node-pty, the hardened runtime with library validation disabled should be fine without additional entitlements. Screen recording doesn't require a specific entitlement key.

The final entitlements list includes allow-jit, allow-unsigned-executable-memory, disable-library-validation, device.audio-input, device.camera, and optionally allow-dyld-environment-variables. step.text: I'm noticing that `pooled(agent)` actually includes the `runs` array with all the steps in the snapshot, which means if a ghost run is still in flight when another user connects, they'd receive that incomplete thread's steps too. That's a potential data leak I need to investigate in the pooled function.

I'm seeing a critical issue with the `pooled()` function where live run steps from in-flight ghost runs leak into snapshots for any client connecting mid-execution. Since steps are keyed only by promptId without thread information, orphaned steps end up stored but invisible in the UI—they'd persist until pruneSteps runs during trimming.

The fix is straightforward: filter out any runs whose prompt belongs to a ghost thread by checking `this.prompts.get(promptId)?.threadId` before including them in `pooled()`. This applies everywhere `pooled()` is used—broadcasts, agent refs—and it's safe because ghost runs should be hidden from everyone unconditionally. The agent's status will still correctly show "working" during ghost prompts (which is honest), but the actual work remains hidden from other clients. step.text:
I'm working out the eye styling for the ghost glyph to match the family—using a radius of 1.05 to align with GameGlyph. The head is centered at (12,10) with radius 7.5, and I'm positioning the eyes at y=9.75 for a friendlier appearance, with x-coordinates at 9.25 and 14.75 to sit slightly off-center horizontally.

Now I'm adding the ghost character to the SVG after GameGlyph. I'm creating a path that draws the head as a rounded shape with a scalloped hem—the classic soft ghost silhouette with bumps hanging downward. The path traces from the bottom left, curves up and around the head, then descends with a series of rounded lobes along the bottom edge before closing. The scallops create that characteristic ghost look, though I'm noticing the cusps where adjacent scallops meet form sharp points that might need smoothing for a more cohesive appearance. Writing wavy hem path... Arcs create cusps at their junctions because the tangents are vertical, so I need to use quarter-arc constructions instead for smooth joins. A cubic Bézier wave is the right approach—I'll define the hem with peak points at y=19 and troughs at y=21.4 running from x=19.5 to x=4.5, positioning control points strategically to create the smooth undulation. I see the issue now — vertical tangents at both peaks and troughs create cusps, which won't work. The wave needs horizontal tangents at the peaks and troughs instead, like a sine curve approximated with quadratic segments, where the control points sit at the peak/trough heights and the joins happen at the midpoints where the tangent crosses horizontally.

The wall-to-wave transition at mid-height will have a slight directional shift (vertical incoming, steep outgoing), which reads as a natural corner like the ghost's shoulder, and with rounded line joins it looks smooth enough. At 16px scale, the visual difference between a true cusp and a smooth join is negligible anyway, especially with `strokeLinejoin="round"` rounding out any sharp points.

Actually, I want to avoid even that zero-angle cusp entirely — I'll make the notches shallower by using arcs with a larger radius and smaller sweep angle, so the tangent directions at the joins aren't vertical. Three lobes spanning 5 pixels each, drawn with a 3.2-pixel radius arc (larger than the 2.5-pixel half-chord), creates a gentler curve that reads as a proper rounded notch rather than a spike.

Let me work out the geometry: with a 3.2-pixel radius and 5-pixel chord, the arc sags about 1.2 pixels down, and the tangent at each endpoint sits at roughly 51 degrees from vertical. That means consecutive lobes meet at a 77-degree angle — a soft V-notch instead of a cusp — which the rounded line join then softens into a proper scallop.

Now I'm adjusting the dimensions to hit a total height of 19. If I increase the lobe sag to 1.5 pixels while keeping the 5-pixel chord, I need a radius of about 2.83 pixels. That steepens the tangent angle to about 62 degrees, which gives a sharper 56-degree interior angle where the lobes meet.

Actually, let me try a gentler curve instead—keeping the sag at 1.2 with a radius of 3.2 gives me a 77-degree tangent angle, which feels better. With the head circle centered at (12, 10) with radius 7.5, the top sits at 2.5 and the walls extend down to 20.3 where the three lobes begin, reaching their bottom at 21.5. This gives me exactly the 19-unit height and 15-unit width I'm aiming for.

Building the SVG path... The dimensions check out—the head and body proportions satisfy the constraints, and the eyes positioned at the center height of the head give it the right ghost-like appearance.

Now I'm adding this as GhostGlyph to the objects file.

… 7 lines left out
@source "<repo>/src/renderer/src";
```

**Why:** Tailwind v4 detects content from the vite root. Importing `styles.css`
directly from a probe outside the repo compiles only the classes used in the probe
file itself, so the component renders completely unstyled and looks broken for a
reason that has nothing to do with the component. `@source` points the scan back at
the real tree.

**How to apply:** Put the probe under `node_modules/.<name>/` so nothing lands in
the auto-committing tree, `npx vite build --config <probe>/vite.config.ts`, then an
Electron main that `loadFile`s the built `dist/index.html`, waits ~1s and writes
`capturePage().toPNG()`. Delete the probe afterwards. Same shape as
`scripts/cover-sheet.mjs`, which is the committed version of this trick.

+ import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, expect, it } from 'vitest'
+ import type { SessionEvent } from '../src/shared/events'
+ import { agentId } from '../src/shared/llm'
+ import { CrewSession } from '../src/server/session'
+ import { Runner } from '../src/runner'
+ import { makeFakeProvider } from './helpers/fake-provider'
+ import { startHost, TestUi, waitUntil, type TestHost } from './helpers/session'
+ import { testRunner } from './helpers/runner'
+ 
+ type ThreadStarted = Extract<SessionEvent, { kind: 'thread.started' }>
+ type AgentEnd = Extract<SessionEvent, { kind: 'agent.end' }>
+ 
+ const settle = () => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 300))
+ 
+ describe('ghost threads', () => {
+   let host: TestHost
+   let runners: Runner[] = []
+   let uis: TestUi[] = []
+ 
+   beforeEach(async () => {
+     host = await startHost()
+   })
+ 
+   afterEach(async () => {
+     for (const ui of uis) ui.close()
+     for (const runner of runners) runner.close()
+     uis = []
+     runners = []
+     await host.close()
+   })
+ 
+   async function connectRunner(name: string, provider = 'fake', label = 'Fake') {
+     const runner = testRunner({
+       name,
+       code: host.code,
+       repoPath: host.repoPath,
+       providers: [makeFakeProvider({}, provider, label)],
+       reconnectDelayMs: 100
+     })
+     runners.push(runner)
+     runner.connect(host.url)
+     await new Promise<void>(resolve => {
+       runner.onStatus = status => {
+         if (status === 'online') resolve()
+       }
+     })
+     return runner
+   }
+ 
+   async function connectUi(name: string) {
+     const ui = await TestUi.connect(host.url, name, host.code)
+     uis.push(ui)
+     return ui
+   }
+ 
+   const fake = agentId('jamel', 'fake')
+ 
+   const about = (ui: TestUi, threadId: string) =>
+     ui.events.filter(e => 'threadId' in e && e.threadId === threadId)
+ 
+   it('/ghost opens a thread the window keeps to itself, and writes none of it down', async () => {
+     const sam = await connectUi('sam')
+     const samSecondWindow = await connectUi('sam')
+     const pat = await connectUi('pat')
+     await connectRunner('jamel')
+     await sam.waitForEvent(e => e.kind === 'agent.online')
+ 
+     sam.chat('@Fake /ghost read the readme', [fake])
+     const thread = (await sam.waitForEvent(e => e.kind === 'thread.started')) as ThreadStarted
+     expect(thread.ghost).toBe(true)
+     // The command itself is not part of the work.
+     expect(thread.title).toBe('@Fake read the readme')
+ 
+     const end = (await sam.waitForEvent(e => e.kind === 'agent.end')) as AgentEnd
+     expect(end.threadId).toBe(thread.threadId)
+     expect(end.text).toContain('read the readme')
+     expect(sam.steps.some(step => step.threadId === thread.threadId)).toBe(true)
+     await settle()
+ 
+     // Nobody else hears any of it, and neither does the same person's other
+     // window: a ghost thread belongs to the one that opened it.
+     for (const other of [samSecondWindow, pat]) {
+       expect(other.events.some(e => e.kind === 'thread.started')).toBe(false)
+       expect(about(other, thread.threadId)).toEqual([])
+       expect(other.steps).toEqual([])
+       expect(other.messages.some(m => m.type === 'queue.state' && m.threadId === thread.threadId)).toBe(false)
+     }
+ 
+     // And a host reading its own log back finds no trace of it.
+     const revived = new CrewSession(host.store).snapshot()
+     expect(revived.events.some(e => 'threadId' in e && e.threadId === thread.threadId)).toBe(false)
+     expect(revived.events.some(e => e.kind === 'message' && e.text.includes('read the readme'))).toBe(false)
+   })
+ 
+   it('an agent picks up where the ghost thread left off', async () => {
+     const sam = await connectUi('sam')
+     await connectRunner('jamel')
+     await sam.waitForEvent(e => e.kind === 'agent.online')
+ 
+     sam.chat('@Fake /ghost read the readme', [fake])
+     const thread = (await sam.waitForEvent(e => e.kind === 'thread.started')) as ThreadStarted
+     await sam.waitForEvent(e => e.kind === 'agent.end')
+ 
+     sam.chat('now the changelog', [], thread.threadId)
+     await waitUntil(() => sam.events.filter(e => e.kind === 'agent.end').length === 2)
+     const second = sam.events.filter((e): e is AgentEnd => e.kind === 'agent.end')[1]
+     // The transcript is kept for the window and nowhere else, so the second turn
+     // still knows what the first one was asked.
+     expect(second.text).toContain('now the changelog')
+     expect(second.text).toContain('read the readme')
+   })
+ 
+   it('a ghost thread is nobody else’s to write in', async () => {

+     const pat = await connectUi('pat')

+

step.text:
Both messages route through the ghost since they carry a threadId. Now I'm working on the AGENTS.md documentation section about ghost threads—I want to explain the concept in plain language without em dashes, covering what the feature does and why it matters. The section describes how `/ghost` creates a private, ephemeral thread scoped to a single window that behaves like any other thread in terms of agent handling and queueing, but leaves no persistent record.

The thread lives in memory keyed to the socket that opened it, similar to how a call works. Events from ghost threads don't flow through the normal emit system to the log or other participants—instead, the event routing checks the thread id and sends ghost events only to that socket while storing them in the thread's own transcript. The three non-event messages (steps, tokens, queue) follow the same pattern through `toThread`. This transcript becomes the context for the agent's next turn, so `threadContext` reads from it rather than the session, giving the ghost thread its own isolated memory. Ghost runs also stay out of the snapshot to prevent mid-run connections from receiving steps they shouldn't see.

When someone else opens a thread, it's protected from being written to via `hiddenFrom` guards on the chat, status, and plan. Closing the window stops whatever was running and drops the transcript, but the entry remains as an empty placeholder since runs completing from the agent's machine still need somewhere to land. The agent's own machine continues the work invisibly in the background rather than being hidden everywhere. Ghost threads display with a dashed stroke and a label to indicate their status.

I should consider whether to document the `/ghost` command—AGENTS.md doesn't have a commands section yet, so this would be new ground but worth including given the persistence rules. Let me tighten this to around six bullets and place it after the "Where a crew lives" section, before "Syncing."

**What it does.** Typing `/ghost` in the chat (anywhere in the line, like `/plan`) opens a thread that belongs to the window it was typed in. Nobody else sees it, none of it is written down, and it is gone when the window is. Everything else is an ordinary thread: an agent takes it, it queues, it steers, and the work it does to the project is real.

**How it stays hidden.** Every event a thread raises carries its id, so one place decides all of it: `emit` hands a ghost's event to that one socket and pushes it onto the thread's own transcript instead of the log. The three thread-scoped messages that are not events, steps, tokens and queue, go through a new `toThread`. Three things I had to close beyond that:

- `threadContext` reads the ghost's transcript, so the agent's next turn in it remembers the last one without the session remembering anything.
- `pooled` leaves a ghost's live run out of the snapshot. Anyone connecting mid-run was otherwise handed its steps.
- `hiddenFrom` guards the chat, the status and the plan, so a thread somebody else opened is not there to be written in however its id was come by.

The window going stops whatever was running and drops the transcript, leaving the entry behind sealed so a late step from the runner has somewhere harmless to land.
